Nine Movies That Influenced Us

In keeping with the title of this article, we present nine movies that made us who we are. These are not our picks for the greatest movies of all time; that would be a different list, and many of the movies discussed here would be left off it.

Admit oneNo. 1 of 9

The Bourne Supremacy

We considered listing the whole trilogy, but ultimately decided to let one movie stand in for the series. The list could have included The Bourne Identity and The Bourne Ultimatum, but Supremacy, the way we see it, is the improved version of Identity: a complete story filled with action, heartbreak and classic espionage.

Like its predecessor and successor, Supremacy was scored by John Powell, who produced a piece of art that complements the story on both an entertaining and an emotional level. The movie takes you on a quest with Jason Bourne as he works out who he is and sets out to avenge someone.

Another great aspect is the way two characters believe they are discussing one subject while they are, in fact, at complete odds. It builds both excitement and realism.

The Bourne movies were not only entertaining; they became the standard and the inspiration for many movies that would not exist, or would look completely different, were it not for the trilogy. Without it, the James Bond franchise would not have changed course towards something more sombre and meaningful, instead of the gadget-heavy and unrealistic fare it had become. John Wick is another movie that borrowed much of its style from the success of films like The Bourne Supremacy.

Transformers

Back in 2007, this movie was already ahead of its time. The way it was made set a standard, a prophecy of what screen culture (television, computers, mobile and cinema) would look like today.

It is your typical Michael Bay movie: boobs, butts, bombs and box office. It shows from the very beginning that it will be fun and overwhelmingly crass, a project built to attract the wider public without complying with standards that would produce dull art pieces instead of putting bums on seats in cinemas. That works for him: he makes studios a lot of money and, in return, they don’t challenge him much about his job.

Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest

There was a point when pirate movies simply did not make the cut in Hollywood. They demanded a lot of administration and, with the technology of the day, looked horrible.

An argument for Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl has a very good chance of convincing us otherwise. However, we still feel that the second instalments of franchises tend to be better films because they build on the success of their predecessors.

Once again, the CGI and VFX were ahead of their time and are still taught to directors today. Pirates was more than a movie; it was a benchmark of how far humanity had come technologically. Each of the main characters had their own agenda, and it played out well, with pacts and betrayals prevalent throughout the film.

Admit oneNo. 4 of 9

Inglourious Basterds

We’ve opted for Inglourious Basterds as the representative of Tarantino’s movies.

The opening scene is one of the greatest in film history; without such a strong introduction, we doubt the movie as a whole would have earned its merit. It takes a serious subject such as the Second World War and adds Tarantino’s own comedic elements. It is very far from being a comedy; instead, it uses comedy to counter the overly stern approach most war movies take.

For many of us, this was the movie that introduced us to Christoph Waltz, who was perfect as a manipulative, entertaining and purely evil character. Tarantino uses Waltz to toy with people, gradually building tension until the people he interrogates break. Tension is what Tarantino creates so expertly. Each scene has purpose and is given weight by characters with their own motivations, motivations we can relate to.

And yes, the Tarantino tropes of gore are present, but they are used sparingly. It’s a different approach, one that lets us tap into his mind as a director rather than being blinded by spectacles of gore.

The Adjustment Bureau

Simply put, The Adjustment Bureau is an art piece. It uses fiction to convey a greater message about sacrifice, adventure and love.

It explores the relationship between free will and destiny. Matt Damon and Emily Blunt are excellent choices for their roles; you are emotionally invested in the desired outcome because the film is written to engage with big concepts and to challenge the audience on what they would do in the circumstances it presents.

Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire

In those days, the books and the movies arrived around the same time, which contributed to the success of both.

The Goblet of Fire began the franchise’s shift towards a darker tone and palette. Put another way, the movies grew up alongside their audience, and J.K. Rowling, who crafted the books in the first place, could chart the way forward for the franchise, winning here and there.

The death of Cedric Diggory is another reason we believe this movie best displays the children’s transition into young adults. Goblet of Fire also expands the world of Harry Potter, introducing new characters with little to no affiliation to Hogwarts.

Bad Boys II

Bad Boys II is one of the best-selling movies on DVD. It is a classic Bay-universe film, where the story sits behind boobs, butts, bombs and box office.

What makes this movie stand out for many of us is the chemistry between Will Smith and Martin Lawrence. Having two Black leads, both in their prime at the time, is another reason it excelled in townships and cities around the world. The comedy, the chaotic presentation and the memorable villains made it easy to sell, which is something no longer as prevalent these days.

Admit oneNo. 8 of 9

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift

Being entertaining is very valuable in the film industry, but being too entertaining can alienate your audience. Tokyo Drift is the best in its series because it is real, grounded and doesn’t abandon its initial target market.

This movie introduced many people to drifting and to Japanese car culture, as well as being a huge advertisement for Japan as a country. There were no larger-than-life actors, which meant the story, told through its characters, was the most critical element. That combination made it a favourite of petrol heads and cinephiles alike.

It is unfortunate that the elements that made Tokyo Drift work were abandoned for profit. The silver lining is that it can be watched alone and the story remains intact.

Admit oneNo. 9 of 9

Casino Royale

The 007 and John Wick franchises owe a lot to the Bourne movies. By the time The Bourne Identity and The Bourne Supremacy arrived, the 007 movies had dropped significantly in quality, almost becoming a caricature of themselves. One of their fatal flaws was that they killed realism, and they got away with it before proper competition in the spy-thriller genre arrived.

Casino Royale was a much-needed reboot for the franchise. Instead of gimmicks, it introduced a Bond who was strong in character, suave and an improvement on recent Bonds.

A perfect example of why it is one of the better Bond movies is that scenes like the poker game slow the action down, leaving room for strong acting and decent dialogue to keep the audience gripped.
